entries.53487678d810eff91ccda5e586af87817acac94c: 1Ki 3:28 <div eID="gen4769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4770" type="x-p"/> This judicial decision convinced all the people that Solomon was endowed with divine wisdom for the administration of justice.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.3"/> <div eID="gen4770" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>yet,</ns0:hi> although he mistook, and miscarried himself in the matter of the High Places, yet in the general, his Heart was right with God, and he both <ns0:hi>loved</ns0:hi> him with in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward Affection, and <ns0:hi>walked</ns0:hi> with him in outward Conversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion and Worship.</ns0:note> Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="5">5 ¶ In Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How could <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> pray in his Dream, or that prayer be acceptable to God, as this was, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> The Dreams of Men are not such insignificant things as many imagine. That good Dreams are oftentimes praise-worthy, and evil Dreams blame-worthy, is not onely the opinion of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and Christians, but of divers of the wiser and bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter <ns0:hi>Heathens;</ns0:hi> and the reason hereof is evident, because mens Dreams are commonly the Images of their minds and tempers, and do onely reflect and represent, though but faintly and imperfectly, those very things which are most imprinted upon their hearts by their waking-meditations, and daily conversation; and therefore it is not unreasonable that either the sinful Dreams of evil-minded Men should be imputed to them, and punished in them, or the vertuous Dreams of good Men imputed to, and rewarded in them; which was <ns0:hi>Solomon's</ns0:hi> case: for his heart having been daily and constantly imployed in passionate longings and prayers for the Wisdom, which here he begs; it was a natural and likely thing that his heart should, as it did, work that way even in his Dreams. Although, to speak truly and strictly, <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s prayer made in his Dream, would have been no way pleasing to God, not profitable to himself, if it had not been the result of his daily and most serious practice; and though God signified his mind in a Dream, yet it was <ns0:hi>Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon</ns0:hi>'s waking-prayers (which were shadowed by this dark representation) which God accepted and required; and this acceptance of God was signified to him in an extraordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary manner, and by a Divine Dream, which was one of those ways whereby God oft used to communicate his Will to his Prophets and People. So the whole business lies thus: <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> Dreamed that God bid him ask what he would, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 3. 5. and that he did ask Wisdom, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6, &c. and that God accepted his desire, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 10. and gave him that Gracious answer, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 11, &c. And all this was done in a Dream, but with this difference; <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s prayer was but imaginary, but Gods answer was real, though conveyed in a Dream. And when he awoke, he knew by Divine inspirati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on that this was a Dream sent from God to assure him that he would give him Wisdom, and Riches, and Honour, and this with respect unto his frequent, constant, and fervent waking-desires, which his Dream of his prayers did suffici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ently intimate. See more on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6.</ns0:note> by night: and God said <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He Dreamed that God said so.</ns0:note>, Ask what I shall give thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:275" />6 And Solomon said <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He Dreamed that he said. See on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. Or, he real<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly said. For although the use of reason is ordinarily so dark and imperfect in Dreams, that such actings are not human actions; yet in extraordinary and Divine Dreams it is but rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonable to allow something extraordinary. For who can doubt but God may so clear up and assist a mans reason in his Dream, that he may have a true and strong apprehension of some things, which also may make a sutable impression upon the will or affections; and consequently such acts of the Soul may be Moral acts, and regardable by God and men? And this might be a kind of exstatical rapture, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by his Soul might be as it were carried out of his Body, as St. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s was, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12. 3. for a season, in which case both his reason might clearly and distinctly apprehend Gods mind, and his Gracious offer; and his Will might make a free choice of Wisdom; which therefore might be accepted and rewarded by God.</ns0:note>, Thou hast shewed unto thy servant David my father great <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> bounty.</ns0:note> mercy, ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording as he walked before thee in truth <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either, First, Sincerely, and without dissimulation. But that is more fully expressed in the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing words, <ns0:hi>in uprightness of heart.</ns0:hi> Or rather, Second<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, in the true Worship and Service of God, in the professi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, belief, practice and defence of the truth, or of the true Religion, or of Gods Will or Word, which is called <ns0:hi>truth, Prov.</ns0:hi> 23. 23. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 17. 17. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 3. 1. So <ns0:hi>truth</ns0:hi> here contains all his duties to God, as <ns0:hi>righteousness</ns0:hi> doth his duties to men, and <ns0:hi>uprightness</ns0:hi> the right manner of performing both sorts of duties.</ns0:note>, and in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with thee <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In thy Judgment, to whom alone his heart was known, and to whom he oft appealed as the wit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of his Integrity; and with respect to whom he perform<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed all his duties, even to men.</ns0:note>, and thou hast kept <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>reserved;</ns0:hi> that which thou didst not reserve for <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> whose Posterity thou didst cut off from the Kingdom.</ns0:note> for him this great kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, that thou hast given him a son to sit on his throne: as <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And now; O LORD my God, thou hast made thy servant king in stead of David my father: and I <ns0:hi>am but</ns0:hi> a little child <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">So he was in Years: not as if he were now but twelve Years old, as many gather from this name of <ns0:hi>Child;</ns0:hi> for that name is given to <ns0:hi>Ishmael,</ns0:hi> when 18 Years old, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 21. 14, 15 and to <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> when 41 Years old, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 7. where the word is the same in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> and before this time <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> calls him <ns0:hi>a wise man, chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 9. but he was now not above 20 Years old; and withal (which he principally in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tends) he was raw and unexperienced, as a Child, in State-Affairs, and altogether unfit for so hard a task.</ns0:note>: I know not <ns0:hi>how</ns0:hi> to go out or come in <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:275" />14 And if thou wilt walk in my ways <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This caution God gives him, lest his great Wisdom should make him proud, or careless, or presumptuous, as if he were out of all danger; and to oblige him to more care and cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cumspection to avoid the snares and mischiefs to which so much prosperity and glory would probably expose him; and withal to justify himself in case he should afterwards alter the course of his Providence towards <ns0:hi>Solomon;</ns0:hi> and that, when men are surprized with <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s dreadful fall, they might know, it was no surprizal to God, but that he did foresee it, and would over-rule it to his own Glory one way or other.</ns0:note>, to keep my statutes, and my commandments, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15. 5.</ns0:note> as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Solomon awoke, and behold, <ns0:hi>it was</ns0:hi> a dream <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="16">16 ¶ Then came there two women <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> harlots <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Victuallers:</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word signifies both. Yet that they were un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />married persons, and so guilty of Fornication, seems most pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, both because there is no mention of any Husbands, whose office it was, if there were any such, to contest for their Wives; and because they lived a solitary life in one House.</ns0:note>, unto the king <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Haply they had presented their Cause to the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferior Courts, who could not determine; and therefore now they bring it to the King, as the Supreme Magistrate, and fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mous for his Wisdom.</ns0:note>, and stood there before him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Desiring and expecting his Sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence in the case.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the one woman said, O my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house, and I was deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of a child with her in the house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And it came to pass the third day <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">So they could not be distinguished by their Age.</ns0:note> after that I was delivered, that the woman was deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered also: and we <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> together; <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> no stranger with us in the house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Therefore no Witness on either side: and although there might be some sensible difference to an exact observer be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween the features of the two Children; yet it is not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable that was much minded by the Neighbours: for though civil Women might assist them both in their Child-births, yet it is not likely they would afterwards converse much with them, as being persons of suspected fame, and the features of the Children, especially for so few days, night easily be so like, that it was difficult to discern the one from the other. And the Testimonies of the Women were of e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />qual credit, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> of none at all.</ns0:note>, save we two in the house.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And this womans child died in the night, because she over-laid it <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And so smothered it: which she justly conjectures, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause there were evidences of that kind of death, but no appearance of any other cause thereof.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And she arose at midnight <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">When I was asleep, as she reasonably and truly con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cluded.</ns0:note>, and took my son from beside me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either, because the really desired the comfort of a Child, to be educated by her, and owned as hers: or, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause she would not be thought guilty of the Childs death, for which she knew not how severely <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> would punish her.</ns0:note>, while thine handmaid slept <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">As the might well know, because had she been a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wake, she had discovered and prevented her design.</ns0:note>, and laid it in her bosome, and laid her dead child in my bosome.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And when I rose in the morning to give my child suck, behold, it was dead: but when I had considered it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, which I did bear.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And the other woman said, Nay, but the li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my son, and the dead <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy son: and this said, No; but the dead <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy son, and the living <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my son. Thus they spake before the king <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Both peremptorily and vehemently affirmed the same thing, oft repeating the same words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Then said the king, The one saith, This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my son that liveth, and thy son <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the dead: and the other saith, Nay; but thy son <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the dead, and my son <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the living.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the king said, Bring me a sword: and they brought a sword before the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And the king said <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">With seeming sincerity and earnestness, though with a design far above the reach of the two Women, or of the People present, who probably with admiration and horror expected the execution of it.</ns0:note>, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 Then spake the woman whose the living child <ns0:hi>was,</ns0:hi> unto the king, (for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. 11. 8.</ns0:note> her bowels <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
